definition: An idiom is a characteristic form of language or style of expression; in this source, it refers to a particular kind of Greek diction that developed through contact between Jewish and Hellenic culture.

provenance.revision: 1901 New York Macmillan original; archive index checked 2026-10-18
provenance.scope: Source record Hellenistic; pinned source text

reasons: The opening general definition (“a characteristic form of language or style of expression”) is not supported by the packet, which only gives a source-specific historical sense of Hellenistic Greek idiom or diction.
The definition should stay within the packet’s narrower sense; the source does not define idiom broadly in general usage.

The packet does not define the term “idiom” itself; it uses the phrase “Greek idiom or diction” as part of an explanation of “Hellenistic,” so the requested sense (“in this source”) for “idiom” is not directly supported.

The definition asserts “a particular kind of Greek diction that developed through contact between Jewish and Hellenic culture,” but the packet specifies this development for “the Greek idiom or diction” only as applying to “Hellenistic,” not as an independent definition of “idiom.”
The definition’s first sentence (“An idiom is a characteristic form of language or style of expression”) is a general linguistic claim not stated in the packet.
